content: An alcohol rub, commonly referred to as a hand sanitizer or healthcare personnel hand wash, is utilized as a supplementary or alternative method to traditional handwashing with soap and water. The active ingredients in alcohol rubs typically include isopropanol, ethanol, or, in some European formulations, propanol. These products are available in various forms, such as gels, foams, and liquid solutions. Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are generally more effective at eliminating germs compared to soap and water, and they tend to cause less skin dryness. When hands are not visibly soiled, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) considers alcohol-based hand sanitizers an acceptable substitute for soap and water in maintaining hand hygiene. For these products to effectively kill microbes, the alcohol concentration must exceed 60%. However, research conducted at East Tennessee State University has revealed that some products sold in American stores contain alcohol concentrations as low as 40%, which are less effective. The optimal alcohol concentration for germicidal activity ranges between 70% and 95%. Alcohol gels with 62% alcohol by volume are less effective at killing germs compared to alcohol rubs with at least 70% alcohol by weight. Formulations combining alcohol with other agents, such as benzalkonium chloride, demonstrate significantly enhanced efficacy compared to alcohol alone. Most alcohol rubs also include moisturizers to prevent excessive drying of the skin. Alcohol rubs are capable of killing a wide range of bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant strains and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. They are also effective against many viruses, such as influenza and the common cold, as well as fungi. However, not all pathogens are equally susceptible. For instance, Clostridium difficile spores are relatively resistant and remain viable despite alcohol exposure. During the anthrax attacks on the United States Postal Service, authorities warned that alcohol-based hand rubs would not be effective against anthrax spores. In environments with high levels of lipids or protein waste, such as food processing facilities, alcohol rubs alone may not suffice for adequate hand hygiene. Alcohol-based gels are flammable and can ignite, producing a dim blue flame due to the alcohol content. Some hand sanitizer gels may not exhibit this effect if they contain high concentrations of water or moisturizing agents. Although rare, there have been documented cases where alcohol hand gels have been implicated in fires, including incidents where static electricity ignited the gel. To reduce the risk of fire, users are advised to rub their hands until the product has dried completely, indicating that the flammable alcohol has evaporated. Additionally, ingestion of alcohol-based hand sanitizers can lead to alcohol poisoning, particularly in young children. In the United States alone, over 12,000 cases of child-related alcohol poisoning have been directly linked to hand sanitizer products.
